meters.label: Hops until the customer is answered

frames.narration: Placing an order touches Payments, Inventory, Shipping, Notify and Analytics. Built with direct calls, Orders calls each in turn and waits: 10 messages and 10 hops, which is 50 ms at an assumed 5 ms a hop.
Payments goes down for 4 ticks at 2 orders per tick. With direct calls the order fails when Payments does: 8 orders fail and 12 complete. The caller is coupled to the callee's availability.
Now Orders publishes OrderPlaced to a broker and subscribers react. The customer is answered after 1 hop (5 ms) and the order is complete after 4 hops (20 ms). It takes 8 messages per order.
The same 4-tick outage loses no orders. The broker queue grows to 8, the longest order waits 4 ticks, and the last one is done at tick 11. All 20 orders complete, but late.

The cost is visibility. The flow is now written in 6 places, and Orders' own code names 0 of its consumers, against 5 with direct calls. Adding a fraud check edits 1 file, but 2 other subscribers of OrderPlaced have to be found and reviewed.

The middle choice is orchestration: one workflow service sends commands and waits. The flow is in 1 place, but it takes 12 messages, and a 4-tick outage with a 2-tick patience fails 4 orders. A longer outage (8 ticks at 3 orders per tick) fails 18.

The over-applied version emits Started and Done events for every step and an audit service listens to all: 23 messages per order, and 3 subscribers to review for the same fraud check. More events did not remove the coupling, they multiplied it.

So use events for facts that several parties react to and that may be late, keep an orchestrator for a sequence with compensation, and give every event an owner, a catalogue entry of its consumers, and a correlation id.
